extracted.intended_audience: general internet users, researchers, moderators, and journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for recognizing, classifying, investigating, and understanding the legal and practical consequences of sock puppet (false) online identities across domains such as reviews, polls, blogs, and state propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a sock puppet / sock puppet account
rubrics_metrics.description: A sock puppet, sock puppet account, or sock is a false online identity used for deceptive purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes online identities created to praise, defend, or support a person or organization, to manipulate public opinion, or to circumvent restrictions such as viewing a social media account that a user is blocked from. The term originally referred to a hand puppet made from a sock; sock puppets are unwelcome in many online communities and forums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Block evasion (type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sockpuppets created to circumvent a block, ban, or other sanctions imposed on the person's original account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This behavior is specifically referenced by Wikipedia policy (see Wikipedia:Block evasion). One reason for creating sockpuppets is to continue participation after being sanctioned under an original identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ballot stuffing / Sybil attacks (type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Creation of multiple identities during online polls or discussions to increase the puppeteer's votes or to present the appearance of majority support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Related to review bombing and reputation-system manipulation; in social-network theory this is called a Sybil attack. Used in stealth marketing and review aggregator manipulation (e.g., Metacritic, Rotten Tomatoes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stealth marketing / fake-support sockpuppets (type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pseudonymous accounts created by marketers or sponsors to pose as independent enthusiastic supporters of a product, book, or ideology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to generate positive testimonials or promote content deceptively; ethically problematic and sometimes legally actionable depending on jurisdiction and facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strawman sockpuppet / strawpuppet (type)
rubrics_metrics.description: A false-flag pseudonym created to make a particular point of view look foolish or unwholesome in order to generate negative sentiment against it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strawman sockpuppets typically behave in an unintelligent, uninformed, or bigoted manner, advancing straw-man arguments that their puppeteers can easily refute. A particular subtype is the 'concern troll'—a false flag pseudonym that pretends to share a group's goals while sowing fear, uncertainty, and doubt (FUD).

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation / detection techniques for sockpuppetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques developed to determine whether accounts are sockpuppets include comparing IP addresses, comparative analysis of writing style, and temporal-based correlation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigators may compare IP addresses (including GeoIP lookups), analyze writing style (stylometry), and look for closely linked posting times. These methods are commonly used by moderators, researchers, and journalists; each technique has caveats (e.g., shared IPs, VPNs, false positives from stylistic similarity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal risk: potential CFAA prosecution in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating or using false online identities has been implicated in prosecutions under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) when alleged to involve 'accessing a computer without authorization'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: United States v. Drew is discussed as an example where prosecutors charged a defendant with CFAA violations for creating a fake MySpace account; the case demonstrates jurisdictional and evidentiary complexities and that convictions under such theories may be contested or dismissed. The presence of terms-of-service violations alone does not guarantee CFAA liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal risk: identity theft, impersonation, harassment charges
rubrics_metrics.description: Sockpuppetry can result in criminal charges such as identity theft, criminal impersonation, and aggravated harassment depending on conduct and jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People v. Golb is cited: use of multiple sockpuppet accounts to attack and impersonate others led to convictions on numerous criminal charges, disbarment, and sentencing—though outcomes vary by case facts and appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil liability: tortious interference and injunctive relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Falsifying multiple identities to post fake comments may constitute tortious interference with business relations and be enjoined by courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New Directions for Young Adults, Inc. v. Davis held that creating multiple fake identities to post comments that create the false impression of many people supporting a position can be wrongful conduct and subject to removal and injunction; the court distinguished between comments that create a false impression of fake people (unprotected) and other speech that may be protected by the First Amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-specific examples indicating unethical/illegal sockpuppetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete patterns of sockpuppetry include corporate executives posting as third parties to praise their companies or attack rivals, authors writing pseudonymous favorable reviews of their own books, journalists posting under false names to attack others, and government/state actors creating personas to influence public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: John Mackey (Whole Foods CEO) posting as 'Rahodeb'; Conrad Black alleged postings in his criminal trial; authors (e.g., Orlando Figes) writing fake Amazon reviews and facing civil damages; journalists suspended for posting under false names. Such conduct often leads to reputational harm and sometimes legal or professional consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-sponsored and large-scale persona management
rubrics_metrics.description: Government or contract operations that create and manage multiple fake online personas to influence net conversations, spread propaganda, or report fabricated events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Operation Earnest Voice (contracted online persona management), the Internet Research Agency (Russian troll farm) and documented state-sponsored influence operations tied to elections. Such activities operate at scale and can be coordinated across platforms and languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and institutional responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Online communities, platforms, and institutions commonly disallow or condemn sockpuppetry and may take actions such as bans, suspensions, cease-and-desist letters, professional discipline, or legal action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wikimedia Foundation explicitly condemned paid advocacy sockpuppeting and banned specific services (e.g., Wiki-PR editing). News organizations and publishers have suspended writers who posted under false names. Courts and regulators may impose injunctions or damages depending on the case.
